pos: n. (Danish reformer, c. 1499–1559; schoolmaster at Viborg, catechist of the Danish Reformation, afterwards superintendent of Funen)
etymology: From Danish Jørgen, the northern form of George, Greek georgos, a husbandman; the surname a Latinised house-name.
biblical_def: Jorgen Sadolin was the schoolmaster of the Danish Reformation. Trained at Wittenberg, he came to Viborg about 1529 and joined himself to Hans Tausen, whose sister he married, and the two men divided the work between them: Tausen preached and Sadolin taught. He opened in Viborg the first evangelical school in Denmark for the training of preachers, and out of that small house came the men who carried the reformed doctrine into the Jutland parishes. In 1532 he put Luther's Small Catechism into Danish, the first catechism the Danish people had in their own speech, and in 1537, when the realm was reformed under Christian III, he was given authority to ordain the new superintendents; he became superintendent of Funen himself the same year. The dictionary records him because he is the plainest Danish instance of the apostolic rule of succession in doctrine rather than in office. Paul does not tell Timothy to guard a chair; he tells him to hand on a deposit to men who will hand it on again: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Sadolin's school was that verse worked out in brick and ink, and the Danish church of the next century was its fruit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer, chiefly in the principles of religion; to teach as to communicate knowledge to one before ignorant; and to edify as to instruct and improve the mind in faith and holiness.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. [Gr. to instruct by asking questions.] A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
TEACH, v.t. To instruct; to inform; to communicate to another the knowledge of that of which he was before ignorant.
SCHOOL, n. [L. schola.] A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages, or any species of learning.
EDIFY, v.t. [L. aedifico.] To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge, in faith and holiness.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Deu 4:9

Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons;
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Eph 4:12
For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:
corruption_summary: The Danish Reformation's schoolmaster, who put the catechism into Danish and trained the preachers Tausen could not train alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that bears on Sadolin is not a redefinition of his name but the quiet abandonment of his work. A church that will not catechise its children has decided, without ever saying so, that doctrine is an adult speciality and that the young need only to be kept interested. The result is a generation that can report what it feels about God and cannot say who God is. Sadolin's answer was a room, a question, and an answer learned by heart, and it held a nation for three hundred years.

The principle to recover is that the faith is taught, not absorbed. Moses binds the duty on the fathers and makes memory the means: “keep thy soul diligently” (Deu 4:9), lest what the eyes have seen depart from the heart. Paul grounds Timothy's whole ministry in a childhood of instruction, “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15), and he names the end of every office in the church as the building of the saints: “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry” (Eph 4:12). Where catechising dies, the ministry has nothing left to perfect.

pos: n. (reformer of Malmo and first evangelical bishop of Lund, c. 1491–1551; translator of the Danish Psalter)
etymology: From Dutch Vormordsen, a patronymic; the given name Frands a Danish form of Francis.
biblical_def: Frands Vormordsen was a Netherlander by birth and a Carmelite by training who came to Denmark with his order and left it for the gospel. Settled at Malmo, then a Danish city in Scania, he became one of the three preachers under whom that town turned evangelical before the realm did. His lasting work was the Psalter. In 1528 he published the Psalms in Danish, the first full book of Scripture the Danes had in their own tongue from a reformer's hand, and he followed it with a Danish primer of devotion. When Scania was reformed he was made the first evangelical bishop of Lund in 1537, holding the oldest archiepiscopal seat of the North as a superintendent under the word rather than a metropolitan over it. The dictionary records him because the Psalter is the church's own answer to the question of what the common people should be given first. Not a system, not a catechism, but the book the Holy Ghost wrote for singing and praying; and the man whose delight is there is the blessed man of the first psalm, for “his delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psa 1:2), and in that law he meditates day and night.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Psalter as the book of Psalms, often separately printed; a psalm as a sacred song or hymn composed on a divine subject and in praise of God; and to sing as to utter sounds with melodious modulations of voice.
webster_full: PSALTER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
SING, v.i. To utter sounds with various inflections or melodious modulations of voice, as fancy may dictate, or according to the notes of a song or tune.
MEDITATE, v.i. [L. meditor.] To dwell on any thing in thought; to contemplate; to study; to turn or revolve any subject in the mind.
corruption_summary: Carmelite turned reformer; gave Denmark its Psalter in 1528 and became the first evangelical bishop of Lund.
scriptures: Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Psa 95:1
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is the displacement of the Psalter from the congregation's mouth. For fifteen centuries the Psalms were the church's songbook; in much of the modern church they are not sung at all, and a believer may pass a lifetime in the pews without once singing the words God gave him to sing. What replaced them is lighter in substance and shorter in memory, and it cannot carry a man through affliction because it was never written for affliction.

The principle to recover is that God has provided the words of praise as well as the object of it. The invitation is corporate and loud: “O come, let us sing unto the LORD” (Psa 95:1). Paul ties the singing to the indwelling word and makes it a means of teaching, not merely of feeling, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16), and he names the inward seat of the music, “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). Vormordsen gave his people that, in their own speech, nine years before their king gave them a reformation.

pos: n. (Danish reformer of Malmo, c. 1490–1552; author of the Malmo Book, the first sustained Danish defence of the Reformation)
etymology: From Danish Laurentsen, son of Laurents, Latin Laurentius, crowned with laurel.
biblical_def: Peder Laurentsen was the pen of the Danish Reformation. A canon who turned evangelical, he led the reforming party at Malmo with Claus Mortensen and Frands Vormordsen, and in 1530 he published the book by which the Danish cause first argued for itself: the Malmo Book, a full defence of what the Malmo congregation had done in abolishing the mass, dissolving the cloisters, and ordering worship in Danish. It is a work of controversy in the best sense. It does not plead for toleration; it states the case from Scripture and invites refutation. Laurentsen also wrote on the Lord's Supper against the Roman sacrifice, and he spent his later years as a schoolmaster in the city he had helped reform. The dictionary records him because he answers a persistent error about the Reformation, that it was a movement of rebellion which argued afterwards. At Malmo the argument came with the act and was published for all to read. Jude requires exactly this of the whole church, that believers “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and the faith contended for is a deposit already given, not a position being invented.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to contend as to strive in opposition or in debate; defence as that which opposes attack or injury; and an apology as a defence, something said or written in vindication of what others think wrong.
webster_full: CONTEND, v.i. [L. contendo.] To strive; to struggle in opposition; to strive in debate; to dispute earnestly.
DEFENCE, n. [L. defensio.] That which opposes attack, violence, danger or injury; any thing that secures the person, the rights or the possessions of men.
APOLOGY, n. [Gr.] A defense; an excuse; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
REASON, v.i. [L. ratio.] To argue; to infer conclusions from premises; to debate; to discourse by way of argument.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Php 1:17
But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel.
Act 17:2
And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures,
corruption_summary: Author of the Malmo Book, 1530, in which the Danish Reformation first argued its own case from Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the conviction that doctrine should not be argued. A church persuaded that contending is in itself unkind will give up every doctrine it cannot defend without discomfort, and will mistake its own silence for charity. Laurentsen's generation had no such illusion. They printed their reasons, named their opponents, and submitted the whole to the judgment of Scripture, which is what a confessional church does when it is healthy.

The principle to recover is that the defence of the faith is a duty laid on every believer and not only on the learned. Peter requires a reason and prescribes the manner of giving it: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), with meekness and fear. Paul understood his imprisonment as an appointment to the same work, “knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel” (Php 1:17), and his method at Thessalonica was argument from the text, for he “three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2).

pos: n. (Danish reformer and hymnwriter, 1499–1575; sang the first evangelical service in Danish and compiled the first Danish hymnbook)
etymology: From Danish Mortensen, son of Morten, Latin Martinus; his byname Tøndebinder, cooper, from his father's trade.
biblical_def: Claus Mortensen was a cooper's son of Malmo, ordained a priest and sent to Wittenberg, who came home and gave the Danish people their first worship in their own language. In 1529 he sang the service in Danish at Malmo, and in the same year he and Hans Olufsen Spandemager brought out the Malmo hymnbook, the earliest Danish evangelical hymnal, with his own translations of Luther and of the old Latin hymns. He was driven out of the city for a time, served at Copenhagen and later again at Malmo, and died there an old man in 1575, having outlived the whole first generation. The dictionary records him because the reformation of worship in the North came by singing before it came by statute. A congregation that can sing the gospel has already confessed it, and the apostle makes the understanding, not the ceremony, the test of edifying song: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also” (1Co 14:15). The hymnbook of 1529 was that verse set to print, and it travelled further than any Danish decree.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song or ode in honour of God; a hymnbook as a collection of hymns; and understanding as the faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity.
HYMN, v.t. To praise in song; to worship by singing hymns.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it, or by which it receives or comprehends the ideas which others express.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
scriptures: What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
Psa 96:1
O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth.
Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
corruption_summary: The cooper's son who sang the first Danish service in 1529 and compiled the first Danish hymnbook the same year.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that touches Mortensen is the separation of music from meaning. Where song is valued for the state it produces rather than the truth it carries, the congregation is gradually relieved of the duty of understanding what it sings, and the words grow thinner to match. The Reformation moved in the opposite direction: it put the words into the people's language precisely so that the singing would be intelligible, and it accepted plainer music as the price.

The principle to recover is that intelligibility governs public worship. Paul will not have even a genuine gift exercised unintelligibly before the assembly, and he states the exchange plainly: in the church “I had rather speak five words with my understanding” (1Co 14:19) than ten thousand in an unknown tongue. The Psalms themselves command the new song and name the place where it is sung, “O sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 96:1), and again, “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1). A hymn the people cannot follow is not yet their praise.

pos: n. (Danish Carmelite and humanist, c. 1485–c. 1534; the ablest Roman opponent of the Danish Reformation)
etymology: From Danish Helgesen, son of Helge; Latinised Paulus Heliae. His nickname Vendekåbe, turncoat.
biblical_def: Poul Helgesen was the most learned Dane of his generation and the Reformation's most serious Danish adversary. A Carmelite prior and lecturer at Copenhagen, he was a reformer of the Erasmian kind: he attacked indulgences, pilgrimages, the ignorance of the clergy, and the abuses of the cloisters, translated Erasmus into Danish, and wanted the Scriptures read. But when the choice came between reforming Rome and leaving her, he would not leave, and he turned his pen against Tausen and the Malmo men with a vigour he had once spent on the abuses. His countrymen gave him the name Vendekåbe, the turncoat, and he disappears from the record about 1534, on the eve of the realm's reformation. The dictionary records him because he is the standing example of the almost-reformer, the man who sees the corruption clearly and will not pay the price of separation. Elijah put the question to such a people at Carmel: “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21). Helgesen never answered it, and the answer he withheld decided his usefulness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to halt as to hesitate, to stand in doubt whether to proceed; lukewarm as moderately warm, and figuratively not ardent, cool, indifferent; and double-minded as unsettled, wavering, undetermined.
webster_full: HALT, v.i. To stop in walking; to hold. To hesitate; to stand in doubt whether to proceed, or what to do.
LUKEWARM, adj. Moderately warm; tepid. Not ardent; not zealous; cool; indifferent.
DOUBLE-MINDED, adj. Having different minds at different times; unsettled; wavering; unstable; undetermined.
INDIFFERENT, adj. Neutral; not inclined to either side, party or opinion; unconcerned; feeling no interest in.
scriptures: Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
Jam 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: The learned Carmelite who attacked Rome's abuses and refused to leave her, and was called the turncoat for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Helgesen embodies is the standing belief that a man may hold the Reformation's criticisms while refusing the Reformation's conclusion. It survives wherever the abuses of a false system are granted freely and the system itself is treated as a home one may improve without leaving. The abuses were never the quarrel. The quarrel was the authority that produced them and the gospel they obscured, and a reformer who will not touch that has conceded the case.

The principle to recover is that the Lord requires a decision and refuses a middle station. He names the lukewarm state and its end: “because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot” (Rev 3:16), he will spue them out. Christ makes the backward look a disqualification, “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:62), and James diagnoses the condition in one line, “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jam 1:8). Joshua set the choice before Israel in the same terms, “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Jos 24:15).

pos: n. (city of Scania, then Danish, now Swedish; the cradle of the Danish Reformation)
etymology: From Old Danish Malmhaug, the gravel mound or ore heap; Swedish Malmö.
biblical_def: Malmo was the first city of the Danish realm to reform itself. A prosperous herring and trading town across the sound from Copenhagen, it had a burgher council willing to act and three preachers willing to lead: Claus Mortensen, Frands Vormordsen, and Peder Laurentsen. Between 1527 and 1530 the town abolished the Latin mass, took the cloisters into civic hands, opened a school, sang the service in Danish, printed the first Danish hymnbook, and published in the Malmo Book a defence of everything it had done. All of this was seven years before Christian III reformed the kingdom from above. The dictionary records Malmo because it shows the ordinary order of the Reformation in the North: a city receives the word, examines it, acts on it, and the realm follows. That is the Berean pattern, and Luke commends it as nobility of a kind the apostles did not find everywhere, for “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), to see whether the things preached were so. A town that will search is a town that can be reformed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town with a corporate government; a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough with the right of a citizen; and to search as to look over or through for the purpose of finding something.
webster_full: CITY, n. [L. civitas.] In a general sense, a large town; a large number of houses and inhabitants, established in one place.
BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town, or one who enjoys the privileges of the place in which he resides.
SEARCH, v.t. [Fr. chercher.] To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to explore; to examine by inspection.
TIDINGS, n. Account of what has taken place, and was not before known; news.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Act 8:8
And there was great joy in that city.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God.
corruption_summary: The Scanian city that reformed itself between 1527 and 1530, seven years before the Danish crown reformed the realm.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer danger is a sentimental reading of the Reformation as a movement of princes and professors in which ordinary congregations were acted upon rather than acting. Malmo refutes it. The council, the preachers, and the townspeople did the work, argued it in print, and bore the risk while the crown was still undecided.

The principle to recover is that the word spreads city by city and is received by hearers who examine it. Luke records the result where it was received, “And there was great joy in that city” (Act 8:8), and the appetite it creates, for on the next sabbath there “came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God” (Act 13:44). Isaiah had long since blessed the men who carry such news over the hills: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7). Malmo heard those feet before Copenhagen did.

pos: n. (city of Funen, Denmark; seat of the diets of 1526, 1527 and 1530 which gave the evangelical preachers legal standing)
etymology: From Old Norse Óðinsvé, the shrine of Odin; a heathen name kept by a Christian city.
biblical_def: Odense is where the Danish Reformation was made lawful. The national assemblies which met in the city in 1526, 1527 and 1530 did not establish the evangelical faith, but they took away the sword from those who would have suppressed it. The Odense recess of 1527 refused the bishops the power to proceed against the preachers and left both parties to preach and be judged by Scripture; the 1530 assembly heard the evangelical ministers present the articles afterwards known as the Confessio Hafnica. The effect was a decade of liberty in which the towns reformed themselves. Odense became an evangelical see under Jorgen Sadolin in 1537. The dictionary records the city because it marks the proper and limited service of the magistrate to the gospel: not to create faith, which he cannot, but to restrain the violence that would silence it. Scripture gives the ground of hope in such seasons, that the ruler is not beyond God's hand, for “as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1), and the church is taught to pray for exactly the quiet which Odense granted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with executive authority; a recess as a withdrawing or retiring, and the decree of a diet; and liberty as freedom from restraint in the exercise of natural rights.
webster_full: MAGISTRATE, n. [L. magistratus.] A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
RECESS, n. [L. recessus.] A withdrawing or retiring; a place of retirement; also, the decree or resolution of a diet of the empire.
LIBERTY, n. [L. libertas.] Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without any restraint but the laws of nature.
KING, n. The chief or sovereign of a nation; a man invested with supreme authority over a nation, tribe or country.
scriptures: Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
corruption_summary: The Danish diets of 1526–1530 met here and left the preachers unmolested; the city became an evangelical see in 1537.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the confusion of the magistrate's office with the church's. Where the state is thought able to establish faith, it will soon be thought able to define it, and a church that has accepted the first will find no ground to refuse the second. Odense did neither. It suspended the coercion and left the preaching to be tried by the text, and the evangelical cause gained more from that restraint than it could have gained from a decree.

The principle to recover is that the Christian prays for civil quiet and obeys God above men when the two collide. Paul directs prayer for rulers to a stated end, “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). He also describes the ruler's normal function, that “rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3). And when a magistrate forbids what God commands, the apostles fix the order of allegiance in a sentence: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

pos: n. (oldest town of Denmark, in south-west Jutland; cathedral city and the see of Hans Tausen from 1542)
etymology: From Old Danish Ribe, probably from a word for the bank or edge of a stream.
biblical_def: Ribe is the oldest town in Denmark and the place where the Danish Reformation grew old gracefully. Hans Tausen, who had preached the gospel at Viborg and Copenhagen and had been the storm-centre of the whole Danish controversy, was made superintendent of Ribe in 1542 and held the office nineteen years until his death in 1561. The Ribe articles drawn up under him in 1542 regulated the worship, discipline and schools of the diocese, and his later years were spent in visitation, catechising and the quiet repair of parishes that had been through twenty years of upheaval. The dictionary records Ribe because it answers a question the Reformation is rarely asked: what does a reformer do after the reformation. Tausen's answer was to become a bishop in the New Testament sense, an overseer who feeds. The office is honourable, and Paul says so without embarrassment: “If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1Ti 3:1). What he must then be, Paul lists; and what he must then do, Paul tells the Ephesian elders in one word, feed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer, a spiritual superintendent or director; an overseer as one who superintends; and to feed as to supply with nourishment, and in a spiritual sense to supply with instruction.
webster_full: BISHOP, n. [Gr. episkopos, an overseer.] An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor.
FEED, v.t. To give food to; to supply with nourishment; in a spiritual sense, to supply with instruction and comfort.
BLAMELESS, adj. Without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure.
scriptures: This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Denmark's oldest town; Hans Tausen's see from 1542 to 1561, where the first reformer became a pastor of pastors.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern reduction of the bishop's office to administration. Where oversight means chiefly the management of property, appointments and reputation, the one qualification the apostle insists on, aptness to teach, becomes optional, and the flock is governed without being fed. The Reformation did not abolish oversight in the North; it required the overseer to preach, and Tausen at Ribe did.

The principle to recover is that the character and the teaching gift are the office's substance. Paul's list begins with character and ends with competence: a bishop must be “blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). He charges the Ephesian elders with the flock on the ground of what it cost, bidding them “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). And Titus is told what an elder must hold if he is to correct error, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).

pos: n. (town of Schleswig; the first territory of the Danish realm to be wholly reformed, and the home of the 1528 Haderslev articles)
etymology: From Old Danish Haderslev, the inheritance or legacy of Hadar; German Hadersleben.
biblical_def: Haderslev was the laboratory of the Danish Reformation. Duke Christian, the eldest son of Frederick I and afterwards Christian III, had been present at Worms as a boy of eighteen and came away convinced. Given Haderslev and Torning as his own in 1525, he reformed them without waiting for the kingdom: he brought in evangelical preachers, suppressed the mass, and in 1528 issued the Haderslev articles, the first evangelical church ordinance in Scandinavia, which set rules for preaching, the sacraments, the conduct of the clergy and the care of the poor. Nine years later the same prince, now king, gave the whole realm a church ordinance drafted with Bugenhagen's help. The dictionary records Haderslev because reformation of doctrine always raises the question of order, and the answer Scripture gives is neither improvisation nor invention. Paul closes his long correction of a disorderly congregation with a single rule: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Order is not the enemy of liberty in worship; it is the form liberty takes when it is governed by the word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority, a permanent rule of action; order as regular disposition or methodical arrangement; and a pattern as an original or model proposed for imitation.
webster_full: ORDINANCE, n. [from ordain.] A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
ORDER, n. [L. ordo.] Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a regular and proper state.
PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar.
DECENT, adj. [L. decens.] Becoming; fit; suitable, in words, behavior, dress and ceremony.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Exo 25:9
According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it.
Heb 8:5

Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
corruption_summary: Duke Christian's own territory, reformed from 1526 and given the first evangelical church ordinance in Scandinavia in 1528.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the notion that order in worship is a matter of taste, to be settled by what gathers a crowd. Once that is granted, the question of what God has commanded is never asked, and the congregation is governed by whatever is currently effective. The reformers of Haderslev asked the other question first, and wrote the answer down where the people could hold their ministers to it.

The principle to recover is the regulative one: the pattern of worship is given, not devised. Paul left Titus in Crete with precisely this commission, “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Under the old covenant God gave Moses no discretion in the matter, directing him to build “after the pattern of the tabernacle” (Exo 25:9) that was shewn him; and Hebrews repeats the charge as the permanent principle, “that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5).

pos: n. (town of central Jutland, Denmark; Hans Tausen's pulpit from 1525 and the first centre of Danish evangelical preaching)
etymology: From Old Norse Víborg, the stronghold by the sacred place; vé, shrine, and borg, fortress.
biblical_def: Viborg was the first Danish town to hear the gospel preached openly and continuously. Hans Tausen, a Johannite monk lately home from Wittenberg, was sent to the priory there about 1525 and began to preach the evangelical doctrine from his own cloister pulpit. He was expelled from his order for it, and the townspeople gave him the church of the Holy Ghost and afterwards one of the grey friars' churches; Jorgen Sadolin joined him and opened the training school. By 1529 the town had abolished the mass in most of its twelve churches. King Frederick I made Tausen his chaplain and so protected him, and the preaching at Viborg ran on through the whole decade of legal uncertainty between the first Odense diet and the reformation of the realm. The dictionary records Viborg because it is the Danish proof of a promise the apostle makes from prison. A preacher can be unfrocked, expelled, and threatened, and the result is only wider circulation, for the chain holds the man and not the message: “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject; a word as an articulate sound expressing an idea; and bonds as that which binds, chains or fetters, and figuratively imprisonment.
webster_full: PREACH, v.i. [L. praedico.] To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a religious text.
WORD, n. An articulate or vocal sound, or a combination of articulate and vocal sounds, uttered by the human voice, and by custom expressing an idea or ideas.
BOND, n. Any thing that binds, as a cord, a chain, a rope; a band. In the plural, imprisonment, captivity.
PULPIT, n. [L. pulpitum.] An elevated place or inclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands.
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Act 5:20
Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
Amo 3:8
The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?
corruption_summary: Tausen's pulpit from about 1525; the first Danish town where the gospel was preached openly and without interruption.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the assumption that the preaching of the word needs a settled legal position before it can do its work. Viborg had none. Tausen preached for twelve years under a protection that was personal, improvised and revocable, and the Jutland parishes were evangelised in that interval.

The principle to recover is that preaching is a necessity laid on the preacher and a liberty no authority can finally revoke. The angel sends the apostles straight back to the place they were arrested in: “Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (Act 5:20). Jeremiah tried to hold the word in and could not, for “his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jer 20:9). Amos reduces the whole matter to a question with one answer: “The lion hath roared, who will not fear?” (Amo 3:8).
